title: A Price Reporting Agency for Trade Materials
one_liner: Turn pooled supply-house invoices into contract-grade, SKU-level price evidence for the trades, starting with cost-change certificates that win price-adjustment change orders and ending as the index that escalation clauses and price-lock guarantees reference.
customer: First: plumbing, HVAC and electrical subcontractors with $3-30M revenue that carry fixed-price bids, multi-month jobs and maintenance agreements and eat cost changes between bid and buy. End state: the counterparties who write and argue escalation clauses, meaning general contractors, property owners and managers, municipal procurement, insurers, home-warranty programs, lenders, and the manufacturers and distributors who want realized-price data.
problem: Price adjustment requests are argued with anecdotes. A sub says copper fittings and water heaters are up 15-20% since the bid, and the GC or owner asks for proof. Broad public benchmarks (producer price indices and estimating books) are category-level and lag what contractors actually pay by SKU at their contractor multiplier in their region, and supplier price letters flow to contractors with a long lag, as the parent's tariff research noted (50% Section 232 copper duty from August 1, 2025). Subs either absorb the difference on fixed-price work or lose weeks assembling invoices by hand. There is no independent, contract-grade reference that both sides of a contract accept, as far as the parent's research and I could find. Parent idea limit: a per-shop audit keeps price data private and never becomes anything a counterparty trusts.
solution: Step 1 (months 0-6) sells a Cost-Change Certificate. For a sub with a fixed-price contract or bid, we parse its own supplier invoices and quotes into a SKU-normalized evidence pack: cost at the bid date versus cost at purchase, supplier price-letter references, invoice copies, and the escalation amount calculated by the contract's own formula, reviewed by the shop's accountant. It needs no network on day one, only one shop's invoices. Step 2: every certificate is paid partly in data, since the shop opts in to contribute its anonymized line items to the pool and in exchange gets a free alert feed ('your PEX-A fitting cost is 9% above the regional median'). Step 3 (months 6-18): publish weekly transaction-based indices by category and region, with a 30-day lag, minimum-contributor thresholds, no supplier or shop names, to stay clear of price-signaling and confidentiality problems. Owners, GCs and municipalities start writing 'adjusted per [Index] Copper Fittings, Region' into contracts and pay for verified access. Step 4 (months 18-36): price-lock guarantees for quoted jobs, underwritten off the index through an MGA or reinsurer partner, where shops pay a small premium on covered materials and we carry the basis risk we understand better than anyone.
why_now: Tariff-driven cost swings made price adjustment a routine dispute in 2025-26, and owners and GCs are rewriting price-adjustment language. The barrier to a transaction index was always normalizing hundreds of supplier catalog and invoice formats into comparable SKUs, and LLMs just made that cheap. Field-service and accounting systems make invoice ingestion easy. The volatility also means the certificate solves a painful, dated, dollar-denominated problem today, not a theoretical data project.
revenue_model: Certificates at $250-400 each, or 15-20% of the escalation actually approved (better alignment on big claims). Then index subscriptions of $500-2,000 per month for GCs, owners, insurers and municipal buyers who want verified reference access, with data licensing to manufacturers and distributors for realized-price and sell-through data. Later underwriting margin on price-lock guarantees, priced at roughly 1.5-3% of covered materials. Example: a sub with a $400K contract that is 30% materials and 8% higher-cost has a $9,600 claim, and a 20% success fee on half of that approved is about $1,000 per contract.
non_obvious_insight: In commodity markets the durable business is not the data feed but being the named reference in contracts, which is why price reporting agencies for metals and lumber have switching costs no feed provider has. The way in is not a dashboard. It is a document that ends an argument, sold to the party who is losing money now. The certificate requires no network on day one, and the network appears as a byproduct because every certificate adds contributed data. It is also a position platform vendors and supply houses structurally cannot take. ServiceTitan and Kojo depend on supplier integrations such as Ferguson and Hajoca, and publishing cross-customer price data pits those partners against their users, while a supply house cannot publish its own multipliers.
first_30_days: Recruit 5 light-commercial mechanical and plumbing subs with open fixed-price contracts where costs have risen since bid (owner peer groups, PHCC and ACCA chapters). Build the SKU normalizer for the top 200 SKUs (copper tube and fittings, PEX, PVC, water heaters, gas flex) across Ferguson, Hajoca, Winsupply, Home Depot Pro and local-house formats. Produce 5 certificates within 2 weeks and record how each GC or owner responds, since approval rate and dollars approved are the key learning. Sign 3 shops to the contingency version. Publish a free monthly 'copper fittings' note from the first shops' data (with disclosure) to seed the brand. Have an attorney review the contribution agreement and the aggregation and lag rules before publishing anything pooled. Web search was unavailable to the parent researcher, so verify that no existing indices or claim-documentation vendors serve this niche.
lineage: mutation of I0068 ('Contingency Audit of Unbilled Plumbing Materials'), type: 10x-or-inverted
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: ServiceTitan Accounts Payable (bill inbox, 3-way matching, Manage Statements, Manage Credits, discrepancy flags), Kojo, BuildOps (Procurement and Payables), Fergus. White space: Nobody I found offers a contingency-fee, done-for-you recovery audit for trade shops. What remains unserved is the customer-side leak: parts on a supply-house ticket with a job name, or pulled from truck stock, that never reached the customer invoice, plus supplier price drift and quoted-price violations tied back to the shop's own pricebook and markup targets. Existing tools (ServiceTitan AP, Kojo, BuildOps, Ramp) are software the shop must adopt and operate, and they focus on paying suppliers correctly. Three parts are open: (1) shops on Housecall Pro, Jobber, FieldEdge or Simpro, or ServiceTitan shops not using Procurement/AP, who have no PO-to-job workflow; (2) the done-for-you, no-recovery-no-fee commercial model, which no software vendor offers; (3) a cross-shop SKU price benchmark from pooled supply-house invoices. I found no evidence anyone has assembled that for residential and light-commercial trade shops. ServiceTitan's Manage Statements and Manage Credits are the closest overlap with the returns-credit and price-error pieces. | How this version avoids them: ServiceTitan AP, Kojo's Sourcing Grid, BuildOps, Ramp and MarginEdge all keep price data private per customer to help that customer buy or pay better. None produces a third-party-verifiable, cross-shop reference that a counterparty accepts, and none sells to GCs, owners, insurers or municipalities. Platform vendors will not publish it because it turns their supplier integration partners (Ferguson is a named ServiceTitan integration) into adversaries. Kojo focuses on larger commercial contractors' purchasing, while this works from the invoices of any shop regardless of field-service software, so Housecall Pro, Jobber and FieldEdge shops are included without any adoption. It also moves the monetization away from the crowded supplier-invoice audit toward evidence and a standard, where the incumbents have no product.

competitors.name: ServiceTitan Accounts Payable (bill inbox, 3-way matching, Manage Statements, Manage Credits, discrepancy flags)
competitors.what_they_do: The dominant field-service platform for mid-size trade shops has an AP module. An automated inbox matches vendor bills to receipts and POs, and 3-way matching flags discrepancies. It captures non-PO bills, tracks vendor statements ('ensure no costs are missed') and vendor credits ('ensure costs are correct'), and says it will 'automatically flag discrepancies and potential fraud'. This directly covers the supplier-billing-error half of the idea (statements, credits, price variance) for any shop already on ServiceTitan. Bill pay is listed as coming Spring 2026. I could not confirm how well it handles supply-house ticket-to-job matching, or whether it reports 'purchased but not billed to the customer'.
competitors.scale_or_funding: ServiceTitan is a public company (NASDAQ: TTAN), with 70+ integrations including Ferguson, per its homepage. This is the strongest overlap and platform-risk threat.

competitors.name: Kojo
competitors.what_they_do: Construction material management for trade contractors. It offers AI invoice scanning, 3-way matching of POs, invoices and delivery slips, and 'supplier billing error detection' ('Only pay for what you receive'). Site claims: save 3.5% on materials, save 3% by catching invoice errors, and a customer that caught $1,200 in supplier billing errors in four weeks. It has 230+ supplier integrations, with Hajoca, Graybar, Wesco, Rexel, Mayer and Border States named as supplier partners. It also has a purchasing 'Sourcing Grid' with side-by-side supplier pricing. It targets larger electrical and mechanical contractors and does not list plumbing or HVAC service shops. It is a procurement and AP system, not a contingency audit, and I found no evidence of a customer-side 'unbilled materials' report.
competitors.scale_or_funding: Well funded. Investors listed on its About page (https://www.usekojo.com/about): Tiger Global, Battery Ventures, 8VC, Schneider Electric, RXR, Tishman Speyer, Suffolk Construction, Bienville, Box Group, Abstract Ventures. Round sizes are not disclosed on the page. It was named to Inc.'s 2024 Best in Business list.

competitors.name: BuildOps (Procurement and Payables)
competitors.what_they_do: Platform for commercial HVAC, plumbing and electrical contractors. Every PO, receipt and bill ties to the job, with 3-way matching ('AP pays only for what arrived'). OpsAI reads receipts and vendor bills and pre-fills them, claiming up to 80% less data entry. Its pages do not mention live supplier price feeds or catalog sync, or any audit of unbilled materials.
competitors.scale_or_funding: Venture-backed vertical SaaS for commercial contractors. Funding not verified in this session. It targets larger commercial shops rather than the $1.5-15M residential and light-commercial segment.

competitors.name: Fergus
competitors.what_they_do: Job management software for plumbers and electricians, mainly in New Zealand and Australia. Its site says 'Get invoices automatically imported and matched to the right job with integrations to the suppliers you use everyday.' This shows that supplier-invoice-to-job auto-matching is already a shipping feature in trade software. Automatic supplier price updates are not mentioned.
competitors.scale_or_funding: Not verified. Regional (ANZ) player, not a US supply-house incumbent.

competitors.name: Ramp AP automation
competitors.what_they_do: General-purpose AP with 2-way and 3-way line-item matching against POs and receipts, to catch overbilling. There is no trades-specific logic, and no documented line-item price-change tracking against prior invoices.
competitors.scale_or_funding: Large fintech. A general-purpose horizontal alternative, not a trade-shop audit.

competitors.name: MarginEdge (restaurant analog)
competitors.what_they_do: Automated invoice line-item capture with alerts on price changes in the most-used products. It proves the model of parsing vendor invoices, tracking SKU price changes and selling that as a subscription. It is not in the trades.
competitors.scale_or_funding: Over 11,000 clients and 5.0M+ invoices processed, per its homepage. Funding not stated on the page.

competitors.name: Housecall Pro, Jobber, FieldEdge (target-customer platforms)
competitors.what_they_do: On the pages I checked, none mentions vendor-invoice matching or supplier price monitoring. Housecall Pro highlights expense cards, invoicing, accounting sync and job costing. Jobber's page (https://getjobber.com/) covers quoting, scheduling, invoicing and AI job-pricing assistance. FieldEdge (https://www.fieldedge.com) offers a flat-rate pricebook and QuickBooks sync, with no supplier price sync mentioned. This is the segment where the idea is least contested, though the platforms could add it later. I checked only their homepages, not help-center docs.
competitors.scale_or_funding: Well-funded platforms (Housecall Pro, Jobber) or a PE-backed one (FieldEdge, part of Xplor). Funding not verified in this session.

What remains unserved is the customer-side leak: parts on a supply-house ticket with a job name, or pulled from truck stock, that never reached the customer invoice, plus supplier price drift and quoted-price violations tied back to the shop's own pricebook and markup targets. Existing tools (ServiceTitan AP, Kojo, BuildOps, Ramp) are software the shop must adopt and operate, and they focus on paying suppliers correctly. Three parts are open: (1) shops on Housecall Pro, Jobber, FieldEdge or Simpro, or ServiceTitan shops not using Procurement/AP, who have no PO-to-job workflow; (2) the done-for-you, no-recovery-no-fee commercial model, which no software vendor offers; (3) a cross-shop SKU price benchmark from pooled supply-house invoices. I found no evidence anyone has assembled that for residential and light-commercial trade shops. ServiceTitan's Manage Statements and Manage Credits are the closest overlap with the returns-credit and price-error pieces.
I0068.evidence_of_demand: No direct evidence found: I could not run any WebSearch (the session budget was exhausted), so no forum complaints, RFPs, or Reddit or Facebook-group threads were located. Nothing I fetched shows shops paying a contingency audit provider. Indirect evidence: (1) ServiceTitan built and markets AP with bill matching, statements and credits tracking, so the vendor with the most trade-shop data judged supplier-invoice reconciliation worth building (https://www.servicetitan.com/features/accounts-payable). (2) Kojo, a well-funded competitor, sells the supplier-error catch as an ROI claim: 'Save 3% by catching invoice errors', a customer catching $1,200 in supplier billing errors in four weeks, and 'Save 3.5% on materials annually' (https://www.usekojo.com/). (3) The tariff price shock is real: the Section 232 proclamation set a 50% duty on the copper content of semi-finished and derivative copper products effective Aug 1, 2025 (https://www.whitehouse.gov/presidential-actions/2025/07/adjusting-imports-of-copper-into-the-united-states/). (4) The restaurant invoice-price-tracking analog shows subscription demand at scale: MarginEdge reports 11,000+ clients and 5.0M+ invoices (https://www.marginedge.com). The idea's own claim that unbilled materials run 'a few percent of revenue' is anecdotal and still unvalidated.
I0068.sharper_angle: Do not pitch 'supplier invoice audit software'. That collides head-on with ServiceTitan AP, Kojo and BuildOps. Position as a done-for-you contingency recovery audit for shops outside the ServiceTitan AP/PO ecosystem: Housecall Pro, Jobber and FieldEdge shops, or ServiceTitan shops that never turned on Procurement/AP, running QuickBooks and buying on account from Ferguson, Hajoca, Winsupply or a local house. Lead with the customer-side leak (materials bought on job tickets or pulled from truck stock but never billed), which the AP-focused competitors do not market. Bundle the supplier-side recoveries (unclaimed return credits, quoted-price violations, tariff surcharges beyond agreed terms). Sell it like sales-tax or freight recovery: fee only on cash recovered, then convert to a low-cost monitoring subscription. Have the shop or its accountant sign off on each recovery, because recovered 'newly captured revenue' is hard to attribute and may be disputed. The moat is the pooled cross-shop SKU price benchmark, which no platform vendor is likely to build because it pits supplier against customer data. Before building, validate on the 10 free audits whether the leak is actually a few percent of revenue. Also check whether ServiceTitan job-costing reports already surface 'PO cost with no billed material', which would erode the wedge in that segment. Treat the verdict as provisional: WebSearch was unavailable, so competitor discovery relied on vendor pages, GitHub and known-vendor probing. Before committing, run manual searches on Crunchbase and Product Hunt, on Reddit r/HVAC, r/Plumbing and r/ServiceTitan, and on 'supply house invoice audit' and 'materials not billed' phrasing, to rule out small funded startups.
